questions.stem:
A 31-year-old man who immigrated from Central America 1 year ago comes to the emergency department with 10 days of fever and right upper quadrant pain. Temperature is 38.9 C (102 F). The liver is tender. Ultrasound shows a single 7-cm hypoechoic lesion in the right lobe. Aspiration yields thick, odorless, reddish-brown fluid, and bacterial cultures of the aspirate are negative. Serum antigen testing for the suspected protozoan is positive. He is started on an oral agent that resolves his fever within 4 days.

Which of the following should be added once that course is complete to prevent relapse and further transmission?

explain.html:
Entamoeba histolytica has two forms with two jobs: the cyst is the infectious form that survives outside the host, and the trophozoite is the invasive form that lyses tissue. Trophozoites can invade the colonic mucosa and travel to the liver, producing a liver abscess whose aspirate looks like "anchovy paste", with fever common and young adult men and immigrants most often affected. Treatment therefore has two steps, one for each form.

This man's single right-lobe abscess with reddish-brown, bacteriologically sterile aspirate and a positive antigen test is extraintestinal amebiasis, and the oral drug that broke his fever is metronidazole, which kills trophozoites. Cysts can remain in the bowel lumen afterward, so a luminal agent such as paromomycin is given second to kill them, which prevents relapse and stops him from shedding infectious cysts to others.
why: Albendazole treats microsporidia and helminths such as Echinococcus, and it does not clear amebic cysts.
Praziquantel treats flukes such as Schistosoma and Clonorchis, not protozoa.
Ivermectin is a roundworm drug and has no place in treating a protozoan like an ameba.
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treats the acid-fast coccidia Cyclospora and Cystoisospora, not amebiasis.
explain.takeaway: Invasive amebiasis is treated with metronidazole to kill trophozoites, followed by a luminal agent such as paromomycin to kill the infectious cysts.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.if_right: a roundworm (nematode) infection rather than a protozoan

rows.why: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treats the acid-fast coccidia Cyclospora and Cystoisospora, not amebiasis.

questions.stem:
A 28-year-old man comes to the clinic with 2 weeks of greasy, foul-smelling stools that float, along with bloating, cramping, and excessive flatulence. He has lost 3 kg. Three weeks ago he went backpacking and drank untreated water from a mountain stream. He has had no fever and no blood in the stool. A stool antigen test identifies a flagellated protozoan.

A biopsy of the proximal small intestine would most likely show which of the following?
choices: Flask-shaped ulcers extending into the submucosa
Noncaseating granulomas throughout the bowel wall
Partial villous atrophy with organisms on the surface
Transmural necrosis with a dense neutrophilic infiltrate

explain.html:
Giardia duodenalis (lamblia) is the most common intestinal protozoan and a flagellate acquired by ingesting cysts, often in water from wells or natural bodies of water. The cyst transmits and the trophozoite causes disease in the small bowel, but it does not invade. The lesion it produces is partial villous atrophy of the jejunum, which shrinks the absorptive surface.

Loss of absorptive surface explains the clinical picture: diarrhea, steatorrhea, flatulence, cramping and bloating, without blood or fever. This backpacker who drank untreated stream water and now has greasy floating stools fits acute giardiasis exactly. Untreated or immunocompromised patients can progress to chronic diarrhea with a malabsorption syndrome, which is why all symptomatic patients are treated (metronidazole or tinidazole first).
explain.table:
FeatureGiardiaE. histolytica
SiteSmall intestine (jejunum)Large intestine
Invasive?NoYes
LesionPartial villous atrophyFlask-like ulcers
StoolFatty, foul, floating, no bloodBloody
First-line drugMetronidazole or tinidazoleMetronidazole, then paromomycin
why: Flask-shaped ulcers are the invasive colonic lesion of E. histolytica, and this patient has no blood in the stool.
Eosinophilic granulomas around eggs are the host response to Schistosoma, a fluke, not a protozoan.
Granulomas of any kind are not part of giardiasis, which causes villous change without inflammation of that type.
Transmural necrosis implies an invasive process, and Giardia trophozoites stay on the surface.
explain.takeaway: Giardia trophozoites are noninvasive but cause partial villous atrophy of the jejunum, producing malabsorptive, foul, floating, nonbloody stools.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Know the clinical syndromes and important sequelae

rows.if_right: bloody diarrhea with trophozoites containing ingested red cells

rows.why: Eosinophilic granulomas around eggs are the host response to Schistosoma, a fluke, not a protozoan.
rows.if_right: freshwater exposure in Africa with eggs and hematuria

questions.stem:
Over 2 weeks in August, 46 children who attended the same community water park develop watery, nonbloody diarrhea with crampy abdominal pain and nausea, starting about a week after their visits. Routine bacterial stool cultures are negative. A modified acid-fast stain of stool shows round oocysts 4 to 7 micrometers in diameter. Health inspectors confirm the pools were chlorinated to recommended levels throughout the outbreak.

Which property of the causative organism best explains this outbreak?
choices: Its spores are inhaled from aerosolized pool water
It requires a snail intermediate host in fresh water
Its oocysts survive standard pool chlorine disinfection
Its larvae penetrate intact skin during swimming
It enters the brain through the cribriform plate

explain.html:
The acid-fast coccidian protozoa (Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Cystoisospora, plus microsporidia) are obligate intracellular parasites diagnosed by acid-fast stain and separated largely by size. Cryptosporidium oocysts measure 4 to 7 micrometers, and the sporulated oocyst is the infectious form, ingested after an incubation of about 7 to 10 days. The oocysts are hardy and resistant to chlorination.

That resistance explains why outbreaks track to drinking water supplies, swimming pools and recreational water facilities, even when those are properly chlorinated, as in this water park cluster. The children's watery, nonbloody diarrhea with cramps and nausea a week after exposure is the usual course, and in healthy hosts it is self-limited. Pool chlorination alone cannot be counted on to prevent these outbreaks.
explain.table:
Acid-fast organismSizeClueTreatment
Microsporidia1 to 2 micrometersSpores in water; chronic diarrhea in AIDSAlbendazole
Cryptosporidium4 to 7Pools, chlorine resistantSelf-limited; nitazoxanide if immunocompromised
Cyclospora8 to 10Imported produce, explosive diarrheaTrimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
Cystoisospora20 to 30 by 10 to 19 (largest)Possible eosinophiliaTrimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
why: Cryptosporidium oocysts are swallowed, not inhaled, and inhalation would not explain an outbreak of diarrhea.
A snail intermediate host is part of every fluke life cycle, not a protozoan one.
Skin penetration during swimming describes Schistosoma cercariae, which cause hematuria or Katayama fever rather than a pool diarrhea outbreak.
Entry through the cribriform plate describes Naegleria fowleri, which causes fatal encephalitis, not diarrhea.
explain.takeaway: Cryptosporidium oocysts (4 to 7 micrometers, acid-fast) resist chlorination, so outbreaks occur in treated pools and water supplies.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Identify life cycle stages relevant to transmission and pathogenesis

rows.if_right: an organism whose spores are acquired from the environment and cause disease by inhalation

rows.why: A snail intermediate host is part of every fluke life cycle, not a protozoan one.
rows.if_right: a fluke such as Schistosoma acquired in snail-infested fresh water

questions.stem:
A 52-year-old woman who received a liver transplant 3 years ago and takes tacrolimus comes to the clinic with 3 weeks of persistent, high-volume watery diarrhea and malaise. She recently returned from a trip during which she swam daily in a hotel pool. She has no fever. Bacterial stool cultures are negative. A combined stool antigen panel is shown.

[[labs 0]]

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
choices: Supportive care alone until it resolves

explain.html:
Cryptosporidium causes a spectrum of disease from asymptomatic infection to mild diarrhea to severe enteritis, and where a patient falls depends on host immunity. Diarrhea can be low or high volume and intermittent or persistent, with malaise, nausea and crampy pain. Diagnosis is a modified acid-fast stain on stool or biopsy, or a stool antigen, as in this panel.

In an immunocompetent host the infection is usually self-limiting. This patient is a liver transplant recipient on tacrolimus with three weeks of high-volume diarrhea after pool exposure, so she is an immunocompromised host, and the treatment for that setting is nitazoxanide. Knowing the host changes management, even when the organism is the same.
explain.table:
ProtozoanFirst-line treatment
E. histolyticaMetronidazole, then paromomycin
GiardiaMetronidazole or tinidazole; nitazoxanide second
CryptosporidiumSelf-limited; nitazoxanide if immunocompromised
Cyclospora, CystoisosporaTrimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
MicrosporidiaAlbendazole
why: Metronidazole followed by paromomycin is the two-step regimen for amebiasis.
Supportive care alone is right for a healthy host, not for a transplant recipient with weeks of high-volume diarrhea.
Albendazole is the treatment for microsporidia, which are 1 to 2 micrometer spores and antigen negative here.
Praziquantel treats flukes, not protozoa.
explain.takeaway: Cryptosporidiosis is self-limited in healthy hosts but is treated with nitazoxanide in immunocompromised patients such as transplant recipients.
explain.topic: Cryptosporidium: treatment in the immunocompromised host

questions.stem:
A 41-year-old man with untreated HIV infection and a CD4 count of 45/microL comes to the clinic with 2 months of chronic watery diarrhea and weight loss. Stool testing for bacteria, viruses, Giardia, and Cryptosporidium antigen is negative. A specialized acid-fast stain of stool shows very small oval spores, about 1 to 2 micrometers in diameter, much smaller than any coccidian oocyst.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this organism?

explain.html:
Microsporidia are intracellular fungi that act like the coccidian protozoa. They exist as spores in water worldwide and cause chronic diarrhea in immunosuppressed patients, especially those with HIV/AIDS. On acid-fast staining their spores are tiny, 1 to 2 micrometers, the smallest of the acid-fast group.

This man with a CD4 count of 45 has two months of watery diarrhea, negative Cryptosporidium antigen, and spores of 1 to 2 micrometers, so size alone separates microsporidia from Cryptosporidium (4 to 7) and Cyclospora (8 to 10). The treatment is albendazole. Getting the size right matters because each member of this group is treated with a different drug.
explain.table:
Acid-fast organismSizeClueTreatment
Microsporidia1 to 2 micrometersSpores in water; chronic diarrhea in AIDSAlbendazole
Cryptosporidium4 to 7Pools, chlorine resistantSelf-limited; nitazoxanide if immunocompromised
Cyclospora8 to 10Imported produce, explosive diarrheaTrimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
Cystoisospora20 to 30 by 10 to 19 (largest)Possible eosinophiliaTrimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
why: Nitazoxanide treats Cryptosporidium, whose oocysts are 4 to 7 micrometers, and the Cryptosporidium antigen here is negative.
Paromomycin is the luminal agent that kills amebic cysts.
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treats Cyclospora and Cystoisospora, whose oocysts are 8 micrometers or larger.
Ivermectin is a roundworm drug and is not used for microsporidia.
explain.takeaway: Microsporidia, fungi that behave like coccidia, show 1 to 2 micrometer acid-fast spores, cause chronic diarrhea in AIDS, and are treated with albendazole.
explain.subject: Microbiology

rows.if_right: clearing E. histolytica cysts after metronidazole

rows.why: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole treats Cyclospora and Cystoisospora, whose oocysts are 8 micrometers or larger.
rows.if_right: acid-fast oocysts of 8 to 10 or 20 to 30 micrometers

rows.if_right: a roundworm (nematode) infection rather than spores in stool

questions.stem:
A 35-year-old woman with poorly controlled HIV infection comes to the clinic with 6 weeks of intermittent watery diarrhea. She grew up in a tropical region and moved to the United States 2 years ago. Complete blood count shows a mild peripheral eosinophilia. A modified acid-fast stain of stool shows large ellipsoidal oocysts measuring about 25 by 15 micrometers.

Which organism is most likely responsible?

explain.html:
The acid-fast coccidian protozoa share a diagnostic method, oocysts on acid-fast stained stool, so size and accompanying clues decide which one is present. Cystoisospora is the largest, at 20 to 30 by 10 to 19 micrometers, and it is found in tropical and subtropical areas. It is the one that may cause eosinophilia, unlike the other acid-fast coccidia.

This woman from a tropical region with poorly controlled HIV, weeks of watery diarrhea, mild eosinophilia and large ellipsoidal oocysts about 25 by 15 micrometers fits Cystoisospora. In immunocompromised patients its course may be protracted. Treatment is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, the same as for Cyclospora.
explain.table:
Acid-fast organismSizeClueTreatment
Microsporidia1 to 2 micrometersSpores in water; chronic diarrhea in AIDSAlbendazole
Cryptosporidium4 to 7Pools, chlorine resistantSelf-limited; nitazoxanide if immunocompromised
Cyclospora8 to 10Imported produce, explosive diarrheaTrimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
Cystoisospora20 to 30 by 10 to 19 (largest)Possible eosinophiliaTrimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
why: Cryptosporidium oocysts are only 4 to 7 micrometers and do not bring eosinophilia.
Cyclospora oocysts are round and 8 to 10 micrometers, far smaller than these.
Giardia is not acid-fast; it is a flagellate found on wet mount, stain or antigen testing.
Microsporidia spores are tiny, 1 to 2 micrometers.
explain.takeaway: Cystoisospora is the largest acid-fast coccidian (20 to 30 micrometers) and, unlike the others, may cause eosinophilia; treat with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

questions.stem:
A 29-year-old field biologist returns from 3 months of work in the rainforest of Peru, where she was bitten repeatedly by small insects at dusk. Six weeks later a papule on her forearm enlarged and ulcerated. On examination there is a 3-cm painless ulcer with a raised, indurated border and a red granular base. There is no fever and no hepatosplenomegaly.

Which of the following is the best way to confirm the diagnosis?
choices: Thick blood smear collected at night
Biopsy of the ulcer's raised outer edge
Culture of the ulcer base for bacterial pathogens

explain.html:
Leishmania is a tissue protozoan transmitted by sand fly bites: the fly injects promastigotes, which become amastigotes inside histiocytes (each with a nucleus and a kinetoplast). In cutaneous leishmaniasis the bite site becomes a papule that ulcerates and enlarges into a painless lesion with a red center and raised border, the "pizza" appearance. It is painless unless bacteria superinfect it.

This biologist's painless, raised-border ulcer weeks after insect bites in the Peruvian rainforest is cutaneous disease, and she has no fever or hepatosplenomegaly to suggest visceral involvement. Diagnosis is a biopsy of the outer edge of the ulcer, where amastigotes are found in tissue, or tissue PCR. Serology and marrow or splenic sampling are reserved for visceral leishmaniasis.
explain.table:
FormPictureDiagnosis
CutaneousPainless ulcer, raised border ("pizza")Biopsy of the ulcer's outer edge, tissue PCR
MucocutaneousYears later, destruction of nose, palate, throat (Central and South America)Tissue diagnosis
Visceral (kala-azar)Fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia, hypergammaglobulinemiaSerology; splenic aspirate or bone marrow
why: Leishmania lives in skin and tissue macrophages, not the gut, so stool O&P will not find it.
A blood smear does not sample the skin ulcer; cutaneous leishmaniasis is confirmed from the ulcer edge and visceral disease from spleen or marrow.
Bacterial culture would only detect superinfection, and this painless ulcer is not superinfected.
Serology is the test for visceral leishmaniasis, not a localized skin ulcer.
explain.takeaway: Cutaneous leishmaniasis is diagnosed by biopsy or PCR of the ulcer's raised outer edge, which shows amastigotes inside histiocytes.

questions.stem:
A 14-year-old boy is brought to the emergency department in July with 2 days of severe headache, fever, and vomiting, and he is now confused. Six days ago he spent the afternoon diving and splashing in a warm, shallow freshwater lake. CT of the head shows diffuse cerebral edema. A wet mount of cerebrospinal fluid shows motile amebae. Despite intensive care he dies 4 days later; autopsy shows hemorrhagic necrosis that is most severe in the olfactory bulbs.

How did the organism most likely reach the central nervous system?
choices: Swallowed water, then spread through the blood
Penetration of the skin, then lymphatic spread
Corneal infection spreading along the optic nerve
Contiguous spread from an infected middle ear
Through the cribriform plate along the olfactory nerves

explain.html:
Naegleria fowleri is a free-living ameba of warm fresh water (rivers, lakes, hot springs) and soil, with infections clustered in summer and in males. It reaches the brain by entering the nose and crossing the cribriform plate along the olfactory nerve; swallowing water does not cause infection. Initial symptoms are headache, fever, nausea and vomiting, and pathology shows cerebral necrosis and edema.

This boy's July lake diving, rapid confusion, diffuse cerebral edema and motile amebae on CSF wet mount are primary amebic encephalitis, and necrosis worst in the olfactory bulbs marks the nasal route. Time from symptom onset to death is about 5 days and mortality is about 97%, with no defined treatment regimen. The route is also the prevention message: keep water out of the nose in warm fresh water.
explain.table:
Free-living amebaEntryHostDisease
Naegleria fowleriNose, cribriform plate, olfactory nerveHealthy swimmers in warm fresh waterPrimary amebic encephalitis, about 97% fatal
AcanthamoebaEye, nasal passages, broken skinContact lens wearers; immunocompromisedKeratitis; granulomatous amebic encephalitis
why: Naegleria is not acquired by swallowing water, and it does not reach the brain through the blood.
Naegleria does not penetrate skin or spread by lymphatics.
Corneal infection describes Acanthamoeba keratitis in contact lens wearers, which does not cause this fulminant illness.
No ameba reaches the brain from an infected middle ear.
explain.takeaway: Naegleria fowleri enters through the nose and crosses the cribriform plate along the olfactory nerve, causing rapidly fatal primary amebic encephalitis after warm freshwater exposure.
explain.topic: Naegleria fowleri: route of CNS entry

explain.objective: Identify life cycle stages relevant to transmission and pathogenesis

questions.stem:
A 23-year-old woman comes to the clinic 5 weeks after returning from a month in Malawi, where she went kayaking and swimming in a freshwater lake. She has fever, hives, facial swelling, a dry cough, and diarrhea. Laboratory studies show:

[[labs 0]]

Three stool and urine examinations for ova are negative.

Which of the following best explains the negative specimens?
choices: The parasite releases eggs only into the blood at night
Humans are accidental hosts in whom the worms cannot fully mature
This hypersensitivity phase occurs before eggs reliably appear
Eggs are laid on the perianal skin rather than in the stool
The organism lives in skin nodules and never reaches viscera

explain.html:
Schistosomiasis has an early and a late diagnostic window. Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever) appears 1 to 2 months after infection, when egg deposition triggers systemic hypersensitivity: fever, urticaria, angioedema, cough, abdominal pain and diarrhea, with eosinophilia and raised AST and alkaline phosphatase. In this phase eggs are not usually seen in specimens.

This kayaker 5 weeks after Lake Malawi has the full syndrome with 34% eosinophils, so her repeatedly negative stool and urine examinations are expected rather than reassuring. Serum antibody becomes the test, positive about 6 to 8 weeks after exposure, and eggs appear in specimens or biopsy later in chronic infection. Treatment is praziquantel.
explain.table:
PhaseTimingPictureBest test
Acute (Katayama fever)1 to 2 months after exposureFever, urticaria, angioedema, cough, diarrhea, eosinophiliaSerum antibody; eggs usually absent
ChronicMonths to yearsGranulomas around eggs: hematuria, portal hypertensionEggs in specimen or biopsy, antibody
why: Schistosoma eggs leave in urine or stool, not into the blood at night, and the timing explains the negative tests.
Humans are definitive hosts for Schistosoma, so the worms do mature; an accidental host is one where the parasite cannot develop and dies.
Perianal egg laying is not a Schistosoma behavior, and this patient has no perianal symptoms.
Schistosomes are blood flukes living in veins, not organisms confined to skin nodules.
explain.takeaway: Katayama fever (fever, urticaria, eosinophilia 1 to 2 months after freshwater exposure) precedes reliable egg shedding, so serology at 6 to 8 weeks is the diagnostic test.
explain.topic: Acute schistosomiasis (Katayama fever): timing of diagnosis
explain.subject: Microbiology

questions.stem:
A 44-year-old woman who raises sheep in a rural area comes to the clinic with 6 weeks of right upper quadrant pain, fever, and malaise. She often eats watercress gathered from a stream that runs through her pasture. Liver enzymes are mildly elevated and eosinophils are 28% (normal 1 to 4). Serology confirms a large liver fluke.

Which of the following is the treatment of choice?

explain.html:
Nearly every fluke in this lecture responds to praziquantel, with one named exception. Fasciola hepatica, the sheep liver fluke, occurs on all continents, is larger than Clonorchis, and is acquired from aquatic vegetation. In the acute phase flukes migrate through the liver, causing RUQ pain, hepatitis and eosinophilia; in the chronic phase they live in the bile ducts and cause biliary fibrosis and obstructive jaundice.

This sheep farmer who eats wild watercress from her pasture stream has RUQ pain, fever, raised liver enzymes and 28% eosinophils, with serology confirming a large liver fluke. Diagnosis rests on serology because eggs in stool are low yield. Fasciola is the only fluke that does not respond to praziquantel, so the drug of choice is triclabendazole.
explain.table:
FlukeSiteAcquired fromKey sequela or clueTreatment
SchistosomaVeins (bladder, liver)Cercariae in fresh waterHematuria, squamous cell bladder cancer; portal hypertensionPraziquantel
Clonorchis, OpisthorchisBile ductsUndercooked fishCholangiocarcinomaPraziquantel
Fasciola hepaticaLiver, bile ductsAquatic vegetationRUQ pain, eosinophilia, obstructive jaundiceTriclabendazole
ParagonimusLungEndemic Asia (also Missouri)Mimics TB; eggs in sputumPraziquantel or triclabendazole
Fasciolopsis buskiIntestineAquatic vegetationLargest fluke, mild GI diseasePraziquantel
why: Praziquantel treats the other flukes, but Fasciola is the one that does not respond to it.
Albendazole treats microsporidia and many tapeworms and roundworms, but triclabendazole is the Fasciola drug.
Ivermectin is a roundworm drug and is not used for flukes.
Metronidazole plus paromomycin treats amebiasis, a protozoan infection.
explain.takeaway: Fasciola hepatica (sheep, watercress, RUQ pain, eosinophilia) is the only fluke that does not respond to praziquantel; it is treated with triclabendazole.

questions.stem:
A 47-year-old man who emigrated from Southeast Asia 1 year ago comes to the clinic with 5 months of chronic cough, intermittent hemoptysis, and pleuritic chest pain. Chest imaging shows patchy infiltrates with small cavities. Three sputum smears for acid-fast bacilli and a mycobacterial culture are negative. Peripheral eosinophils are 14% (normal 1 to 4). Bronchoalveolar lavage shows operculated eggs.

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

explain.html:
The lung fluke Paragonimus westermani is found in Southeast Asia and Japan (with P. kellicotti in Missouri). The early phase, within 2 months of exposure, brings fever, diarrhea, abdominal pain, urticaria and cough. Larvae then penetrate the diaphragm and migrate within the pleural cavity, causing chest pain, cough and malaise, and the late phase brings inflammation, fibrosis and hemoptysis.

Because it mimics tuberculosis, the deciding findings here are negative acid-fast smears and culture, peripheral eosinophilia, and eggs in bronchoalveolar lavage in an emigrant from Southeast Asia. Diagnosis is eggs in sputum, lavage or stool, and treatment is praziquantel or triclabendazole. Thinking of it prevents months of unnecessary TB therapy.

questions.stem:
A 24-year-old woman returns from 3 months of volunteer work in rural South Asia with 5 days of cramping abdominal pain and frequent small-volume stools streaked with blood. Colonoscopy shows scattered ulcers with raised edges. Biopsy shows ulcers that are narrow at the mucosal surface and widen in the submucosa, containing motile organisms with a single nucleus, a central karyosome, and ingested red blood cells. Her roommate, who shared her meals and drinking water, is entirely asymptomatic.

Which of the following best describes how this organism was transmitted to the patient?
choices: Skin penetration by larvae from soil
Bite of an infected sand fly
Inhalation of spores in household dust
Ingestion of cysts in fecally contaminated water
Eating trophozoites in undercooked pork or beef products

explain.html:
For the intestinal protozoa, the cyst survives harsh environmental conditions and is the infectious form, while the trophozoite is the motile, reproductive, invasive form. Entamoeba histolytica is acquired by ingesting cysts through fecal-oral spread, contaminated water or food, or oral-anal contact, and humans are its only host. Trophozoites then adhere in the large intestine and either colonize the mucosa and shed new cysts or invade the submucosa and spread laterally, producing flask-like ulcers.

This traveler's biopsy shows flask-shaped ulcers with trophozoites that have a central karyosome and ingested red blood cells, which identifies the organism. Her roommate who shared the same water is well because about 90% of infections are asymptomatic and may only shed cysts, which is how the infection keeps spreading.
why: Larvae penetrating skin from soil is not an amebic route; amebae are swallowed as cysts.
Sand flies transmit Leishmania, a tissue protozoan, not an intestinal ameba.
Spores in dust or water fit microsporidia, and amebae are not inhaled.
Trophozoites do not survive outside the host and are not the infectious form, and amebiasis is not a meat-borne infection.
explain.takeaway: The cyst is the infectious form of Entamoeba histolytica, spread fecal-orally, while the trophozoite invades tissue and causes flask-shaped colonic ulcers.
explain.subject: Microbiology
explain.objective: Identify life cycle stages relevant to transmission and pathogenesis

questions.stem:
A 38-year-old man taking an anti-tumor necrosis factor biologic comes to the clinic with 6 days of explosive watery diarrhea, fatigue, and a 2-kg weight loss, preceded by a day of low-grade fever. Two coworkers who ate with him at a restaurant 9 days ago have the same symptoms; all three ate a salad of fresh imported berries and herbs. Bacterial cultures are negative. An acid-fast stain of stool shows round oocysts measuring 8 to 10 micrometers.

Which of the following is the treatment of choice?

explain.html:
The acid-fast coccidia are told apart by size and source: microsporidia 1 to 2 micrometers, Cryptosporidium 4 to 7, Cyclospora 8 to 10, and Cystoisospora the largest at 20 to 30. Cyclospora oocysts contaminate vegetation, classically imported lettuce, herbs and fruit, then invade small intestinal epithelium and reproduce. The diarrhea can be explosive, with weight loss, and can persist for up to 3 months.

This cluster of three diners who shared imported berries and herbs, with a febrile prodrome, explosive watery diarrhea and round 8 to 10 micrometer acid-fast oocysts, is Cyclospora. Treatment of choice is trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, the same drug used for Cystoisospora. The food history plus oocyst size is usually enough to name the organism before any other test.
explain.table:
Acid-fast organismSizeClueTreatment

Cryptosporidium4 to 7Pools, chlorine resistantSelf-limited; nitazoxanide if immunocompromised
Cyclospora8 to 10Imported produce, explosive diarrheaTrimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
Cystoisospora20 to 30 by 10 to 19 (largest)Possible eosinophiliaTrimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole
why: Nitazoxanide is for Cryptosporidium in immunocompromised hosts and second line for Giardia, not Cyclospora.
Metronidazole followed by paromomycin treats amebiasis, not an acid-fast coccidian.
Albendazole treats microsporidia, which are 1 to 2 micrometers, far smaller than these oocysts.
Tinidazole is a first-line Giardia drug, and Giardia is not acid-fast.
explain.takeaway: Cyclospora (8 to 10 micrometer acid-fast oocysts) comes from imported fresh produce, causes explosive diarrhea, and is treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole.

questions.stem:
A 26-year-old man who moved from Bangladesh 4 months ago comes to the clinic with 2 months of intermittent fever, night sweats, and a 7-kg weight loss. His skin has darkened. The liver is palpable 3 cm and the spleen 10 cm below the costal margins. Laboratory studies show:

[[labs 0]]

A bone marrow aspirate would most likely show which of the following?
choices: Trophozoites containing ingested red blood cells
Amastigotes with a kinetoplast inside macrophages
Acid-fast oocysts within marrow stromal cells
Microfilariae circulating in the marrow sinusoids

explain.html:
Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar, "black fever") involves the liver, spleen and bone marrow, has an incubation of 2 to 6 months, and 90% of cases come from India, Bangladesh, Nepal, Sudan and Brazil. Its disease pentad is fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia and hypergammaglobulinemia. It can also be an opportunistic infection in AIDS.

This recent immigrant from Bangladesh has every element: fever, a 7-kg weight loss, a palpable liver and massive spleen, pancytopenia, and high total protein with low albumin, which signals hypergammaglobulinemia. Because the parasite lives in macrophages of the marrow and spleen, a bone marrow biopsy or splenic aspirate shows amastigotes with a nucleus and kinetoplast inside macrophages; serology also helps. First-line treatment is pentavalent antimony, with liposomal amphotericin B second.
why: Trophozoites with ingested red cells describe E. histolytica in colonic tissue, not marrow.
Acid-fast oocysts are intestinal coccidia found in stool, not in marrow.
Nothing in this pentad points to a filarial worm; the findings localize to macrophage-rich organs.
Caseating granulomas with acid-fast bacilli would mean tuberculosis, a bacterial infection.
explain.takeaway: Visceral leishmaniasis presents with fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia and hypergammaglobulinemia and shows amastigotes in macrophages on bone marrow or splenic aspirate.

explain.objective: Know the clinical syndromes and important sequelae

rows.if_right: bloody diarrhea or a liver abscess with "anchovy paste" aspirate

rows.if_right: watery diarrhea with acid-fast oocysts in stool

questions.stem:
A 30-year-old woman who wears soft contact lenses comes to the clinic with 10 days of severe left eye pain, photophobia, tearing, and a foreign-body sensation. She rinses her lenses in tap water and wore them while swimming in a hotel pool 3 weeks ago. Slit-lamp examination shows a ring-shaped corneal infiltrate. PCR of corneal scrapings identifies a free-living ameba that can encyst in heavily chlorinated or hot water.

In a patient with advanced AIDS, this same organism is most likely to cause which of the following?
choices: Fulminant meningoencephalitis after warm lake diving
Flask-shaped colonic ulcers with bloody diarrhea
Chronic watery diarrhea from small bowel invasion
Granulomatous amebic encephalitis with high mortality

explain.html:
Acanthamoeba is a free-living ameba ubiquitous in water that encysts under extreme conditions such as heavy chlorine or high temperature, which is why lens solutions and pool water do not reliably kill it. It enters through the eye, nasal passages or broken skin. Which disease it causes depends on the host.

In immunocompetent contact lens wearers, like this woman who rinses lenses in tap water and swam with them in, it causes keratitis, diagnosed by PCR of corneal scrapings. In immunocompromised patients, such as someone with advanced AIDS, the same organism causes granulomatous amebic encephalitis, which carries a high mortality, and can disseminate to skin and lungs. There is no definite treatment regimen.
explain.table:
Free-living amebaEntryHostDisease
Naegleria fowleriNose, cribriform plateHealthy swimmers in warm fresh waterPrimary amebic encephalitis, about 97% fatal
AcanthamoebaEye, nasal passages, broken skinContact lens wearersKeratitis
AcanthamoebaSameImmunocompromisedGranulomatous amebic encephalitis, disseminated skin and lung disease
why: Fulminant meningoencephalitis after diving in a warm lake is Naegleria fowleri, which strikes healthy hosts.
Hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia and high globulin are the visceral leishmaniasis pentad.
Flask-shaped colonic ulcers with bloody diarrhea describe E. histolytica.
Chronic watery diarrhea in AIDS fits Cryptosporidium or microsporidia, which are intestinal, not free-living amebae of the eye.
explain.takeaway: Acanthamoeba causes keratitis in immunocompetent contact lens wearers and granulomatous amebic encephalitis with high mortality in immunocompromised patients.

questions.stem:
A 34-year-old man who grew up near a freshwater lake in East Africa, where he fished and swam daily as a child, comes to the clinic with several months of dysuria and intermittent painless hematuria. Urinalysis shows many red blood cells. Cystoscopy shows sandy patches and nodules in the bladder wall, and biopsy shows eggs surrounded by an eosinophilic granulomatous reaction.

If this infection continues untreated for decades, he is at greatest risk for which of the following?
choices: Squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder

explain.html:
Trematode life cycles always involve water and snails. In schistosomiasis (bilharzia), snails release cercariae, the infectious form, which penetrate skin in fresh water; the adults are blood flukes that live in veins. Disease comes from the host's eosinophilic granulomatous response to deposited eggs, not from the worms themselves.

This man with childhood freshwater exposure in East Africa, months of hematuria and dysuria, and bladder biopsy showing eggs with eosinophilic granulomas has urinary schistosomiasis. Decades of egg-driven inflammation in the bladder wall lead to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder, the sequela tied to Schistosoma, while hepatic disease leads instead to portal hypertension. Diagnosis is serum antibody or eggs in specimens after 6 to 8 weeks, and treatment is praziquantel.

explain.takeaway: Chronic urinary schistosomiasis, driven by eosinophilic granulomas around deposited eggs, predisposes to squamous cell carcinoma of the bladder.

questions.stem:
A 58-year-old man who grew up in southern China comes to the clinic with 2 months of painless jaundice, pruritus, and weight loss. Since childhood he has regularly eaten raw, lightly pickled freshwater fish. Imaging shows dilated intrahepatic bile ducts and a mass at the hepatic duct bifurcation. Stool microscopy shows small operculated eggs, and a peripheral eosinophilia is present.

Which of the following best explains the development of the mass?
choices: Adult flukes in the bile ducts cause chronic inflammation
Larvae migrate from lungs into the liver and encyst
Eggs embolize to portal venules and cause cirrhosis
A hydatid cyst grows slowly within the right lobe
Trophozoites invade from the colon by way of the portal vein

explain.html:
The liver flukes Clonorchis sinensis (Chinese liver fluke) and Opisthorchis are acquired by eating undercooked freshwater fish, especially carp, in eastern Asia, southern China and Vietnam. Metacercariae move from the small intestine into the bile ducts and mature, and adults can live up to 50 years, laying eggs that pass in stool. Adults in the bile duct provoke an inflammatory reaction that leads to fibrosis.

Chronic infection brings biliary obstruction and gallstones and, over decades, cholangiocarcinoma. This man from southern China who has eaten raw pickled fish since childhood has painless jaundice, dilated intrahepatic ducts, a mass at the hepatic duct bifurcation, operculated eggs in stool and eosinophilia. Diagnosis is stool eggs (from about 4 weeks after infection) with eosinophilia, and treatment is praziquantel.

Fasciola hepaticaLiver, bile ductsAquatic vegetationRUQ pain, eosinophilia, obstructive jaundiceTriclabendazole

Eggs causing portal hypertension and cirrhosis describe hepatic schistosomiasis, not a fluke living in the bile ducts.
A hydatid cyst comes from Echinococcus eggs passed by dogs, not from raw fish, and it does not form a bile duct mass.
Trophozoites reaching the liver from the colon cause an amebic abscess with "anchovy paste", not a bile duct cancer.
explain.takeaway: Clonorchis and Opisthorchis, acquired from undercooked freshwater fish, live in the bile ducts, cause inflammation and fibrosis, and predispose to cholangiocarcinoma; treat with praziquantel.

questions.stem:
A 50-year-old man from rural Bolivia comes to the clinic with 1 year of nasal stuffiness, nosebleeds, and progressive difficulty swallowing. Examination shows destruction of the nasal septum with a collapsed nasal bridge and ulceration of the soft palate. On his shin is an old, flat, atrophic scar; he says that site was a painless, slowly enlarging ulcer with a raised border after insect bites in the jungle 15 years ago, which eventually healed on its own.

Which vector transmitted the organism responsible?

explain.html:
Leishmania is a tissue protozoan transmitted by sand flies, which inject promastigotes that become amastigotes inside macrophages; every clinical form follows that same bite. Cutaneous disease is a papule that ulcerates into a painless lesion with a raised border. Mucocutaneous disease is caused by species in Central and South America and manifests years to decades later with destructive lesions of the nose, epiglottis and throat.

This Bolivian man's old atrophic shin scar from a painless raised-border ulcer after jungle insect bites, followed 15 years later by nasal septum destruction, a collapsed nasal bridge and palatal ulceration with dysphagia, is mucocutaneous leishmaniasis. The vector is the sand fly. Treatment depends on species and disease, with pentavalent antimony first line.
why: Mosquitoes do not transmit Leishmania; the sand fly does.
Black flies are not the Leishmania vector.
Chrysops (deer) flies are not the Leishmania vector.
Snails are the intermediate host for every fluke, not a vector for a protozoan like Leishmania.
explain.takeaway: Mucocutaneous leishmaniasis (Central and South American species) follows a skin ulcer by years to decades and destroys the nose and palate; all Leishmania are transmitted by sand flies.
